articles.title: Vishal Bhardwaj, Shaunak Sen-Mentored Co-Production Fund Picks Ladakh-Set ‘Kakthet’ as Winner (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Stenzin Tankyong’s debut feature “Kakthet” (Idiot), set in the remote high-altitude region of Ladakh, has been selected as the winner of the inaugural INR40 lakh ($42,000) feature film co-production fund run by Humans of Cinema and Safarnaama Pictures.
body: The Ladakhi-language project was selected from nearly 400 entries after an extensive screening and evaluation process.

Tankyong has spent eight years making films that bring Ladakh’s stories, landscapes and culture to international audiences. His short films “Sekool” (2019) and “Last Days of Summer” (2023) have screened at festivals including the International Film Festival Rotterdam, the Clermont-Ferrand International Short Film Festival and the Dharamshala International Film Festival.

“Kakthet” is produced by Ritu Sarin and Rajesh Thanickan, alongside French co-producers La Belle Affaire Productions. A filmmaker and producer whose career spans more than 30 years, Sarin co-founded both White Crane Films and the Dharamshala International Film Festival. Thanickan’s credits include Neeraj Ghaywan’s “Homebound,” executive produced by Martin Scorsese and premiered at Cannes in 2025; “Santosh,” which premiered at Cannes in 2024; and “Our Share of Sand,” which premiered at the 2026 Venice International Film Festival’s International Critics’ Week, where it won the Audience Award.

articles.title: Peter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88
articles.summary: The film-maker enjoyed a long and varied film and TV career, from horror movies and true-crime thrillers to Cannibal and Breaking Bad. Peter Medak, the British-Hungarian director of The Changeling, The Krays and Let Him Have It, has died aged 88.
body: Medak enjoyed a long and varied career across film and TV, which included spirit-of-the-times classics A Day in the Death of Joe Egg and The Ruling Class (both from 1972), cult horror The Changeling with George C Scott, and The Krays and Let Him Have It, period true crime films made in the early 1990s. He also directed numerous episodes of high-profile TV drama, including the 80s revival of The Twilight Zone, Homicide: Life on the Street, and Hannibal.

Medak pivoted back to TV and, starting in 1994, directed six episodes of acclaimed cop series Homicide: Life on the Street, and followed it up by directing an episode of The Wire in 2002. Later TV work included episodes of high-profile shows such as House, Breaking Bad and Cannibal.

articles.title: Alexander Payne Hit With Copyright Suit Over ‘The Holdovers’ Script
articles.summary: A screenwriter sued Alexander Payne on Wednesday, alleging that the script for “The Holdovers” was based on his unproduced screenplay set at a children’s hospital. The screenwriter, Simon Stephenson, took his allegations to the Writers Guild of America in 2024, but was advised that the union could…
body: In addition to Payne, the lawsuit names as defendants “Holdovers” screenwriter David Hemingson, producer Mark Johnson, Miramax, Focus Features, and other corporate entities.

The suit contends that there are 46 “matched incidents” in the plots of the two scripts. As described in the complaint, Stephenson’s script, “Frisco,” tells the story of a dispirited doctor at the hospital who is stuck looking after a precocious teenage patient. The two develop a friendship on a trip to San Francisco, culminating in the doctor’s decision to quit his job and set off on a cross-country trek.

The lawsuit argues that the similarities with “The Holdovers” are more than mere coincidence, and that the structure and incidents of “Frisco” “were meticulously transposed into ‘The Holdovers,’ with surface cosmetic details changed.”
“Screenplays are often called the blueprint for a film,” the lawsuit states. “The Defendants built their film using ‘Frisco’ as their blueprint.”

articles.title: ‘Lord of the Rings,’ ‘Spider-Man’ Digital-Human Pioneer Remington Scott to Head Eros Imagination (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: The Hollywood technologist who led Gollum’s motion capture on “The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers” and built the first digital humans made with Light Stage technology for “Spider-Man 2” will run Eros Imagination, a new creative technology and experiences business set up by Eros Innovation.
body: The new outfit will mix human artists with visual effects, AI, digital-human tools, real-time production and games. Beyond serving Eros’ own businesses, it will go after deals with outside studios, streamers, filmmakers, game developers, musicians, estates and rights holders. It will work next to Eros Brahmand, the group’s film and content studio, and supply technology and production support for films, series, franchises and live immersive shows. Planned services run from AI-assisted filmmaking and post-production to immersive concerts, virtual production and playable game characters.

One of its first projects centers on Mohammed Rafi, the celebrated Indian playback singer. Eros has a signed deal with Rafi’s family, and the plan is an immersive music experience that combines an authorized digital performance with cinematic storytelling, high-end visuals and audience interaction. The project depends on rights and creative approvals. Eros said it is meant to introduce Rafi’s music to younger audiences. It will also give the unit digital-human and production workflows that it could reuse with other authorized artists and properties.

articles.title: ‘Pixels and Pencils’ Panelists Talk the Dangers of AI, Demanding Animation Processes and the Importance of Human Creativity
articles.summary: As artificial intelligence continues to advance, animators are increasingly facing questions about the future of their craft and the role of human creativity in filmmaking. But the majority are not interested in letting AI into their art of storytelling.
body: Meg Weichman, the artistic manager of SCAD’s Theatres and Festivals, introduced this year’s panel, which she described as a celebration of the “imagination, artistry and collaboration that brings extraordinary animated stories to life.”
But to make something “extraordinary” requires significant effort, which is part of what makes the process “magical,” Chong said.

“Every set, every character, every piece of cloth, every piece of hair, every moment of atmosphere, all of that is created and made from ground zero. There’s no camera you can point at,” Chong told the audience. “It’s just completely fabricated and made and created, and that’s a pretty amazing thing, because that’s one of the reasons why I think these movies take so long, is because they have to create their own world.”

Creating an animated film typically takes well over a year — and sometimes much, more more. From the first idea to its big-screen release, Bird’s “Ray Gunn” took roughly 30 years to finalize, though he wasn’t consistently working on the film throughout that period.

articles.title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence
articles.summary: Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’ An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.
body: The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.

The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.
A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.

Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.

articles.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
articles.summary: The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs.
body: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.

articles.title: The Devils review – Ken Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale is a frenzied aria of confrontation and hysteria
articles.summary: Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave put in the performances of their lives in this film originally banned for obscenity that highlights the violence of power. ‘I could never be Satan’s boy.
body: ‘I could never be Satan’s boy. I haven’t the humility.” The speaker is Father Urbain Grandier, the 17th-century French priest accused of witchcraft, stylishly played by Oliver Reed, in Ken Russell’s scabrous 1971 classic; it is now restored and rereleased in its complete form after years of censorship. It comes from an era when movies, playing in high-street cinemas, still had the power to shock, to position that shock in the polite cultural mainstream and to compel serious discussion about whether that shock – or, conversely, a ban – was justified.

Reed is a revelation with his intelligent, focused, charismatic and dignified performance as the sensualist cleric who submits to injustice like a dissolute version of Thomas Becket. Grandier is a magnetically handsome man and de facto municipal leader of the town of Loudun in western France, bullishly promoting its independence, its walls and fortifications; this is to the rage of Cardinal Richelieu (Christopher Logue) and the Catholic church, who suspect that it will become a sanctuary and power-base for Huguenots and Protestants.

articles.title: Film buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger?
articles.summary: Since 1994, Turner Classic Movies has been a haven for old film lovers. Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future. I have made many attempts to lessen the existential disaster we call Tuesday – tacos, trivia – but lately only one thing works.
body: Every Tuesday in October, Alicia Malone, an affable Australian film historian wearing business casual and a flippy bob, introduces a double feature. These are often midcentury melodramas featuring striking leads, serpentine plots, and the burnt hues of fall rendered in indulgent Technicolor. Like All That Heaven Allows (1955), about a widow who finds herself crushed under the weight of 1950s suburban conformity – and the teeny waistline of her swing skirts – while nursing a crush on her much-younger gardener. Or Leave Her to Heaven (1945), about a beautiful socialite so obsessed with her hapless husband that she will kill anyone who threatens their bond.

In these films, everyone has their original teeth and no one takes Ozempic. It’s my weekly break from doomscrolling, from whatever- maxxing, from the maddening norm of vertical content. I want to live in the world of Sweater Weather cinema all year long.

Now with Skydance’s David Ellison calling the shots, fans are panicking over its unclear future.

articles.title: Babydoll singer says life will 'never be the same again' after UK number one
articles.summary: The singer is finding genuine joy in life again after a difficult period led to him quitting music.
body: Jamie Miller says "nothing feels normal" anymore but he is trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song Babydoll.
Last week the 29-year-old became the first Welsh artist to top the UK singles chart in 15 years with the viral TikTok hit.

The singer, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, said his dreams had "come true" and life would "never be the same again" after a challenging few years in which he even had to give up on music for a time.
Miller said the last year had been "insane" as he has gone from watching Gavin and Stacey with his parents to getting messages on his social media from the cast.

articles.title: Sam Fender pre-sale moved after 'bot attack'
articles.summary: Fender says a "sophisticated" attack affected a website selling tickets for his Newcastle shows.
body: Sam Fender has rescheduled the pre-sale for his tour's homecoming show after a "sophisticated bot attack" reportedly affected a ticketing website.

In a post on Instagram, the 32-year-old said he had been told the site Gigantic had been hit for his shows at St James' Park in Newcastle in summer 2027, prompting him to move the sale back 24 hours to 09:30 GMT on Thursday.
It came days after he removed a ticket category from sale due to his unhappiness with the costs for fans, which he said were out of his control.
Gigantic said its system had detected an "unusually high volume of suspicious activity" resulting in error messages on its site and it had halted the pre-sale to protect fans.
